planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring; Revival is a blight-resistant American-Chinese hybrid chestnut bred for precocious bearing and needs a second, genetically distinct chestnut nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct chestnut trees for reliable cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Revival is an American-Chinese hybrid chestnut developed as part of the blight-resistant breeding lineage that also produced the well-known Dunstan chestnut, combining some of the American chestnut's tree form and nut quality with the Chinese chestnut's resistance to chestnut blight. Trees bear precociously, often within a few years of planting, and produce medium to large, sweet nuts that drop free of the burr for easy harvest in fall. Because it carries genuine blight resistance rather than simply avoidance, Revival can be planted with more confidence in areas with a history of chestnut blight pressure than pure American chestnut. Good heat tolerance makes it a reasonable choice for Gulf South food-forest and small-orchard plantings, though as with all chestnuts, well-drained soil and good air circulation help minimize disease pressure in humid summers.
sources: Chestnut Growers of America variety notes
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — Chestnut Cultivar Trials

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Dragon fruit is an epiphytic cactus that needs a sturdy support structure and, for most cultivars, night-time hand pollination to guarantee fruit set.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Purple Haze is a dragon fruit cultivar grown for its deep magenta-purple flesh, one of the most intensely colored selections available, with a sweeter, more aromatic flavor profile than the classic white-fleshed types. As an epiphytic cactus it needs a sturdy post or trellis to climb and support its long, three-ribbed, succulent stems, along with excellent drainage rather than the regular watering a conventional fruit tree would need. Flowers open at night and close by dawn, so for best fruit set hand-pollinate after dark by transferring pollen with a small brush between open flowers, since many dragon fruit selections are only partially self-fertile. Zone 9 gardeners in the warmest, most frost-protected locations can attempt in-ground planting, but most should grow Purple Haze in a large container that can be moved to a sheltered spot whenever a freeze threatens, since even brief cold exposure damages the succulent stems.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit Production in Florida
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Dragon Fruit for South Texas
California Rare Fruit Growers — Hylocereus and Selenicereus Varieties

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Palora is a self-fertile yellow dragon fruit selection from Ecuador prized for its exceptionally sweet flavor compared to red-skinned types.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Palora is a yellow-skinned dragon fruit selection originally from Ecuador, grown for fruit that is generally sweeter and more intensely flavored than red-skinned Selenicereus undatus types, with crisp white flesh and small edible black seeds. Unlike many dragon fruit cultivars, Palora is self-fertile and does not require hand pollination or a second plant to set fruit, which simplifies home cultivation, though the spiny, ridged yellow skin needs more careful handling at harvest than smooth-skinned red types. As an epiphytic cactus, give it a sturdy post or trellis to climb and cactus-like watering rather than the frequent irrigation a conventional fruit tree would need. Palora is generally slower-growing and somewhat more cold-sensitive than red dragon fruit types, so zone 9 gardeners should plan on container culture with winter shelter rather than in-ground planting except in the very warmest, most protected microclimates.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit Production in Florida
California Rare Fruit Growers — Hylocereus and Selenicereus Varieties
